The why

What’s Driving The Path

Why Physiotherapy And Performance Coaching?

I'm genuinely fascinated by anatomy, by sport, and by what it takes to help someone rebuild and grow them into the best possible version of themselves as an athlete. That interest isn't just theoretical — throughout my teenage years playing, I picked up injury after injury and became a regular face in the physio's chair. Being on that side of the table so often is what showed me I don't just want to treat an injury and hand an athlete back to their coach. I want to be part of both ends — the clinical work that gets someone right, and the training work that gets them better than they were before.

Why This Pathway?

I chose to build the science degree first so I'd have the full picture — anatomy, physiology, biomechanics — before specialising in either direction. ASCA Level 1 comes next so I can start coaching real athletes while I'm still studying, instead of waiting until I'm fully qualified to get in the room. The Master's in High Performance Sport & Physiotherapy is what lets me actually practice clinically at the level I want to work at — pitch-side, with elite athletes.

Before the classroom

National Athletics, then the NPL system

Athlete → Practitioner

My experience as a footballer has shaped my interest in understanding performance from both sides: experiencing training and competition as an athlete while developing the scientific knowledge to assess, program and support athletes as a practitioner. Years of training and competing in Sydney's NPL system showed me what separates athletes who come back from injury well from those who don't — and that gap is exactly what I'm training to close.

Before I set my sights on physiotherapy and coaching, I competed as a national-level athlete in athletics for a number of years — track and field gave me an early, firsthand look at what serious training and competition actually demands. I later moved into football, playing in the NPL (National Premier Leagues) system here in Sydney, where I saw up close what separates athletes who come back well from injury from those who don't. Between the two, that's a big part of why I'm building toward a career that sits right at that intersection.

Where clinical meets performance

Three Disciplines, One Athlete

Musculoskeletal Conditions

The clinical foundation — understanding injury, assessment, and rehabilitation of the musculoskeletal system as the basis for safe return-to-sport decisions.

Strength & Conditioning

The performance side — programming and coaching physical preparation for athletes training in high performance environments.

Sports Injuries

Recognising and managing acute and overuse injuries on the field, then building the return-to-play plan that gets an athlete back to full training safely.

My goal: understand the entire athlete pathway, not just one stage of it.

Try it yourself

Give Me An Athlete

Pick an athlete and I'll walk through how I'd think about their training — the same assess, investigate, program, monitor framework used across sport science.

Football · Winger
Goal: Get faster
I'd assess
10m acceleration→30m sprint→CMJ→RSI→lower-body strength

Wingers rely on short, sharp bursts more than top-end speed, so I'd start with 10m acceleration to capture how quickly they get out of the blocks, then 30m to see how that acceleration carries into a fuller sprint. A countermovement jump (CMJ) shows how much force they produce through the legs in a single explosive action, and reactive strength index (RSI) — jump height divided by ground contact time — shows how well they reuse that force elastically, which matters every time they plant and cut. Lower-body strength testing gives me the strength foundation everything else is built on.

I'd investigate
Acceleration mechanics→max-velocity exposure→horizontal force→reactive strength

From those numbers I'd dig into acceleration mechanics — shin angles, ground contact time, and how much force is applied horizontally rather than vertically, since horizontal force production is what separates good accelerators from average ones. I'd also look at how much max-velocity running the winger actually gets exposed to in games and training, because if they rarely reach top speed in matches, that's a training gap rather than a talent ceiling. Reactive strength ties back into how efficiently they absorb and redirect force when cutting past a defender.

I'd program
Sprint training→resisted acceleration→plyometrics→strength/power

The program would combine short-distance sprint work with resisted acceleration — sled pushes or resisted sprints — to build horizontal force production specifically. Plyometrics (bounds, hops, depth jumps) develop the reactive strength picked up in testing, and traditional strength/power work (squats, hip thrusts, jump variations) underpins both. I'd sequence these so strength work supports the sprint and plyo sessions rather than competing with them for recovery.

I'd monitor
Sprint splits→CMJ→session RPE→wellness→training exposure

Ongoing sprint splits tell me if the training is actually transferring to speed, and repeat CMJ testing tracks whether power output is trending up or dropping — a red flag for fatigue or overreaching. Session RPE and wellness checks (sleep, soreness, mood) capture the athlete's internal response to the load, and tracking total training exposure makes sure I'm not accidentally overloading a winger who's also playing full matches on the weekend.

Rugby · Winger
Goal: Improve repeat sprint ability
I'd assess
30m sprint→repeated sprint test→CMJ→lower-body strength→Yo-Yo IR1

A single 30m sprint tells me raw speed, but rugby wingers need to repeat that speed multiple times a game, so I'd add a repeated sprint test — something like 6 x 30m with short recoveries — to see how much their times drop off across efforts. CMJ and lower-body strength give me the power and strength base, and the Yo-Yo Intermittent Recovery Test (IR1) shows how well their aerobic system supports repeated high-intensity efforts, since aerobic fitness underpins recovery between sprints more than people expect.

I'd investigate
Phosphocreatine recovery→lactate tolerance→aerobic contribution→fatigue in sprint mechanics

The key question is why performance drops off across repeated efforts. That often comes down to phosphocreatine (PCr) recovery — the fast energy system used in each sprint needs roughly 3–5 minutes to fully restore, which a rugby match rarely allows — so I'd look at how well the athlete tolerates incomplete recovery. Lactate tolerance and the aerobic contribution to repeated efforts both matter here too, and I'd watch whether sprint mechanics start to break down under fatigue, since that's often where injuries creep in.

I'd program
Repeated sprint training→short-recovery intervals→aerobic base work→strength/power maintenance

Repeated sprint training itself — sets of short sprints with match-realistic recovery windows — is the most specific way to build this quality, alongside short-recovery interval running to stress the same energy systems. I wouldn't neglect the aerobic base, since a stronger aerobic engine speeds up recovery between efforts, and I'd keep a maintenance dose of strength and power work running alongside so raw sprint speed doesn't slide backwards while repeatability improves.

I'd monitor
Sprint decrement (fatigue index)→session RPE→GPS high-speed running→wellness

The clearest marker is the sprint decrement score — the percentage drop-off across repeated sprints — which should improve as the program takes effect. I'd track session RPE to gauge how hard these sessions feel relative to prescribed intensity, use GPS data to monitor high-speed running in games and training, and keep an eye on wellness markers, since repeated-sprint work is some of the most fatiguing training there is.

Football · Midfielder
Goal: Improve aerobic capacity
I'd assess
Yo-Yo Intermittent Recovery Test→resting & submax heart rate→body composition

The Yo-Yo Intermittent Recovery Test is my go-to here because it mimics the stop-start nature of match running far better than a straight run, and it estimates aerobic capacity for field sport athletes specifically. I'd pair that with resting and submaximal heart rate, which track cardiovascular fitness over time without needing a lab, and body composition, since carrying unnecessary mass makes covering the same match distance more costly.

I'd investigate
Aerobic base→lactate threshold→running economy→match running demands

Beyond a single fitness number, I'd want to understand the aerobic base being trained, the lactate threshold — the intensity at which the body shifts to relying more on anaerobic metabolism — and running economy, which is how efficiently the athlete uses oxygen at a given pace. I'd also look at match-running data where available: total distance, high-speed running, and how output changes across the two halves, since a second-half drop-off often points at an aerobic limitation rather than a tactical one.

I'd program
Aerobic interval training→tempo runs→small-sided games→progressive overload

Aerobic interval training — long intervals at high intensity with incomplete recovery — is a time-efficient way to shift the aerobic ceiling, and I'd add tempo runs at a controlled pace to build the aerobic base without excessive fatigue. Small-sided games train match-specific aerobic and anaerobic demands simultaneously while keeping the ball involved, which matters for buy-in. All of this sits on progressive overload — gradually increasing volume or intensity so the aerobic system is forced to adapt without tipping into overtraining.

I'd monitor
Yo-Yo re-test→heart rate response→GPS training load→session RPE

A Yo-Yo re-test after a training block is the clearest way to confirm aerobic capacity has actually improved. I'd also track heart rate response to a fixed training stimulus over time — a lower heart rate for the same effort is a strong sign of aerobic adaptation — alongside GPS-derived training load and session RPE to make sure the prescribed dose matches what the athlete is actually absorbing.

Football · Returning from injury
Goal: Rehab a hamstring injury
I'd assess
Hamstring strength test→Nordic curl strength→single-leg hop test→range of motion→sprint mechanics

Hamstring strength testing — using a handheld dynamometer or isokinetic device where available — gives an objective number rather than relying on how the athlete feels, and I'd compare it directly against the uninjured side. Nordic curl strength specifically is one of the better-supported markers for hamstring injury risk in the research, so I'd track that closely. Single-leg hop testing checks whether the leg can tolerate load and produce force safely, range of motion confirms the injury site has settled, and sprint mechanics show whether the athlete is compensating or protecting the leg without realising it.

I'd investigate
Strength deficit vs uninjured side→eccentric capacity→movement compensations→readiness to sprint

The core question through rehab is always the same: how big is the gap between the injured and uninjured side, and is it closing? I'd track the strength deficit directly, with particular attention to eccentric hamstring capacity — the muscle's ability to lengthen under load, which is exactly the action that causes most hamstring strains during sprinting. I'd also watch for movement compensations that develop while protecting the injury, since those often become their own problem later, and assess genuine readiness to sprint at high speed rather than assuming time alone means the tissue is ready.

I'd program
Progressive loading→isometric to eccentric work→graduated return-to-sprint→change-of-direction reintroduction

Rehab has to be progressive and criteria-based rather than following a fixed calendar. I'd start with isometric holds to reintroduce load safely, move into eccentric-focused work — Nordic curls are a staple given the research behind them — and only then build toward a graduated return-to-sprint protocol that increases speed and volume in controlled steps. Change-of-direction work comes back once straight-line sprinting is solid, since cutting places different demands on the hamstring, and full training integration is the last step, not the first.

I'd monitor
Limb symmetry index→sprint exposure→pain & soreness→RPE→return-to-play criteria

The limb symmetry index — comparing injured to uninjured side across strength and hop tests — is the clearest objective marker of readiness, and I wouldn't clear a return to full training until that gap has closed to an acceptable range. I'd track sprint exposure carefully as speed is reintroduced, monitor pain and soreness after each session, use RPE to see how hard the athlete is finding each stage, and apply clear return-to-play criteria rather than a gut feeling before signing off on full training or match involvement.

Netball · Goal Attack
Goal: Improve change-of-direction speed
I'd assess
5-0-5 agility test→single-leg hop test→CMJ→RSI→lower-body strength

The 5-0-5 agility test is built specifically to measure deceleration and change-of-direction speed rather than straight-line speed, which fits netball's constant cutting and stopping far better than a standard sprint test. Single-leg hop testing and CMJ give me a picture of unilateral and bilateral power, RSI shows how efficiently that power is used elastically during quick ground contacts, and lower-body strength testing underpins the whole picture, since netball's landing and cutting demands are heavily strength-dependent.

I'd investigate
Deceleration mechanics→cutting technique→landing control→hip/knee stability

Netball has one of the highest non-contact ACL injury rates of any sport, largely from repeated landing and cutting under fatigue, so I'd pay close attention to deceleration mechanics — how well the athlete controls their body when slowing down — and cutting technique, particularly whether the knee tracks in line with the foot or collapses inward. Landing control on single-leg contacts and hip and knee stability more broadly are both central here, since weaknesses in either are strongly linked to injury risk as well as performance.

I'd program
Change-of-direction drills→deceleration training→plyometrics→single-leg strength work

Change-of-direction drills that progressively add reaction and decision-making, rather than pre-planned cutting patterns, build the specific quality netball demands, and I'd pair that with deliberate deceleration training, since most athletes train acceleration far more than they train stopping safely and efficiently. Plyometrics build the elastic power picked up in RSI testing, and single-leg strength work — split squats, single-leg Romanian deadlifts — directly targets the landing and cutting stability that protects the knee while also improving performance.

I'd monitor
5-0-5 times→landing quality→session RPE→wellness→training exposure

Re-testing 5-0-5 times over the training block shows whether change-of-direction speed is actually improving, and I'd track landing quality — through video review or simple qualitative screening — since technique can improve even before the numbers move. Session RPE and wellness monitoring apply here as much as anywhere, and I'd track total training exposure, particularly cumulative jump and cutting volume, since that's where overuse issues tend to build up in netball athletes.
